title: The Essential Points of Chan Practice, Annotated
author: Zhanran
excerpt: (From the Collection of Dream Wanderings: Instructions on the Essentials of Chan Practice)

inline.s: (From the Collection of Dream Wanderings: Instructions on the Essentials of Chan Practice)

[The school of Chan transmits the Buddha's mind-seal, and this is no small matter. It began when Bodhidharma came from the West and established the principle of single transmission, imprinting the mind with the four fascicles of the Lankavatara. Thus, though Chan is a special transmission outside the teachings, it is in fact verified by the teachings, and only then is the non-dual path of the Buddha and the patriarchs seen.]

The school of Chan transmits the mind-seal of the Buddha, and this is no small matter. It began when the Patriarch Bodhidharma came from India (ancient India) and established the principle of single transmission, imprinting the mind with the four fascicles of the Lankavatara Sutra. Therefore, although Chan is a special transmission outside the teachings, it is in fact verified by the teachings (the Tathagata's word-teachings), and only then is the non-dual path of the Buddha and the patriarchs seen.

[Mind-seal] 'Mind' is the Buddha-mind; 'seal' has the meaning of approval or imprinting. The Chan school does not establish written words nor rely on speech; it transmits mind by mind alone, imprinting the Buddha-mind upon the minds of sentient beings, realizing the non-dual mark. [Single transmission] The meaning of transmitting alone, purely and singly. In teaching, the Chan school relies not on words or writing but takes up one-to-one transmission, striking at the moment of opportunity to transmit the Dharma of the mind-seal; this is called 'the single transmission of the mind-seal.'
The Blue Cliff Record says:
'Bodhidharma, gazing from afar upon this land
(China)
and perceiving that it possessed faculties for the Mahayana, crossed the sea and came, transmitting alone the mind-seal.'
[A special transmission outside the teachings] This means the particular transmission that lies outside the Tathagata's word-teachings.

[The work of investigation also issues from the teachings. The Lankavatara Sutra says: 'Sitting in meditation amid the mountains, cultivating in the upper, middle, and lower grades, one can see the flowing stream of the deluded thoughts of one's own mind.' This is truly the World-Honored One's direct instruction on the essential method of doing the work. It also says: 'That mind-consciousness, the false marks of the self-nature realms that appear from one's own mind — the sea of birth and death, karma, craving, and ignorance, all such causes — are wholly transcended.' This is the Tathagata's direct instruction on the wonderful purport of awakening the mind. It also says: 'The sages of old, handed down one to another, saw that deluded thoughts have no self-nature.' This, again, is the direct instruction of the secret mind-seal. This is the essential point at which the yellow-faced old man (the Buddha) taught people to investigate Chan.]

The Chan school's work of investigation also issues forth from the scriptural teachings. The Lankavatara Sutra says: 'Sitting in meditation amid the mountains, cultivating in the upper, middle, and lower grades, one can see the flowing stream of the deluded thoughts of one's own mind.' This is truly the World-Honored One's direct instruction on the essential method of doing the work. It also says: 'That mind-consciousness, the false marks of the self-nature realms appearing from one's own mind; the sea of birth and death, karma, craving, and ignorance — all such causes are wholly transcended.' This is the World-Honored One's direct instruction on the wonderful purport of awakening the mind. It also says: 'The sages of old, transmitted one to another, saw that deluded thoughts have no self-nature (deluded thoughts are illusory).' This, again, is the World-Honored One's direct, clear instruction on the secret mind-seal. This is the essential point at which Shakyamuni Buddha taught people to investigate Chan.
[The yellow-faced old man] This refers to Shakyamuni Buddha, because the Buddha's body appears with a golden-yellow hue. [All such causes are wholly transcended] The scripture passage is:
'Sitting in meditation amid the mountains, cultivating in the lower, middle, and upper grades,
one can see the flowing stream of the deluded thoughts of one's own mind.

In countless lands all the Buddhas pour the consecration, attaining the power of ease, spiritual powers, and samadhi, together with all good teachers and the Buddha's sons and attendants. That mind-consciousness, the false thoughts of the self-nature realms that appear from one's own mind; the sea of birth and death, karma, craving, and ignorance — all such causes are wholly transcended.'

[When Bodhidharma instructed the Second Patriarch, he said: 'You have only to extinguish all conditions outside and, within, have no panting of the mind; make the mind like a wall, and you can enter the path.' This was the essential method Bodhidharma first revealed for people to investigate. When the teaching reached Huangmei (Hongren), who was seeking an heir, the Sixth Patriarch had barely spoken 'originally there is not a single thing' when he received the robe and bowl — this is the true purport of the transmitted mind-seal. And when the Sixth Patriarch returned south and instructed Daoming, he said: 'Think neither of good nor of evil; at just this very moment, what is the Original Face of the venerable Ming?' This was the Sixth Patriarch's first essential instruction for people to investigate.]

When the Patriarch Bodhidharma instructed the Second Patriarch Huike, he said: 'You have only to extinguish all conditions outside and, within, have no panting of the mind; make the mind like a wall, and you can enter the path.' This was the essential method the Patriarch Bodhidharma first revealed for students to investigate. When the teaching reached the Fifth Patriarch as he sought an heir, the Sixth Patriarch had barely uttered 'originally there is not a single thing' when he received the robe and the bowl — this is the true purport of the transmitted mind-seal. And when the Sixth Patriarch returned south and instructed Huiming, he said: 'Think neither of good nor of evil; at just this very moment, what is the Original Face of the venerable Ming?' This was the essential instruction the Sixth Patriarch first revealed for people to investigate; he opened the way for the study of the huatou.

[Extinguish all conditions outside, no panting of mind within, make the mind like a wall — this says: outside, put down all conditions; within, the mind does not cling to any state; the mind should be like a wall with no crack or crevice, so that no dharma enters — that is, states cannot move the mind; only thus can one enter the path. [Huangmei] Refers to the Fifth Patriarch of the Chan school, Hongren, so called because he dwelt at the Dongchan Monastery on Huangmei Mountain. [Daoming] This is Huiming in the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, who, being instructed by the Sixth Patriarch, greatly awakened and honored Huineng as his teacher; to avoid the 'Hui' character of his teacher's name, he changed his own name to Daoming. [Leading the way] The Record of Rites, 'Chapter on Learning,' says: 'When the kings of the three dynasties sacrificed to the rivers, they always sacrificed first to the Yellow River and then to the sea.' The ancients held the Yellow River to be the source of the sea, so the sovereigns first sacrificed to it and then to the sea. The phrase 'leading the way' later came to denote the first thing that initiates an endeavor.

[From this we know that the Buddhas and patriarchs of old only taught people to awaken to their own mind and to recognize themselves; never was there any talk of a gongan (koan) or a huatou. It was after Nanyue and Qingyuan that the patriarchs, adapting to circumstances, gave instruction, mostly striking where doubt arose, and making people turn their heads and that was all. Even those who did not understand, though the tongs and hammers were applied, were simply left to the conditions and causes of the time. It was Huangbo who first taught people to look at a huatou; and it was not until the master Dahui that it was strongly advocated, teaching students to investigate a single gongan of the ancients as a handle, called the huatou, and urging them to hold it up relentlessly.]

From this we know that the Buddhas and patriarchs of old only taught people to awaken to their own mind and to recognize themselves; there was never any talk of a gongan or a huatou. It was only after Nanyue and Qingyuan that the patriarchs, adapting to circumstances, gave instruction, mostly striking at the place of doubt and making people turn their heads, and that was all. Even those who did not understand, though they were hammered and forged, were simply left to the conditions and causes of their time. It was the Chan master Huangbo who first taught people to look at the word 'wu' (nothing) as a huatou; and it was only at the time of Dahui that it was strongly advocated, teaching students to investigate a single gongan of the ancients as a handle, which is called the huatou, urging people to hold it up relentlessly.

[Nanyue and Qingyuan] Descending from the Sixth Patriarch Huineng came the two great Dharma lineages of Nanyue (Chan master Huairang) and Qingyuan (Chan master Xingsi). The lineage of Nanyue produced the Linji (Rinzai) school; the lineage of Qingyuan produced the Caodong (Soto) school. [Tongs and hammers] The blacksmith's tools; practice is often likened to a hundred refinings into steel; the 'refining' here is hammering. Through repeated hammering the impurities in the iron blank are removed and its structure improved, turning it into a fine steel implement.
A sword that cuts iron as if it were mud and severs a hair blown against its edge is made by a thousand such hammerings.

[Huangbo] The Tang dynasty Chan master Xiyun (Duanji), who left home at Huangbo Mountain in Fuzhou while young and later attended the great master Baizhang Huaihai of Jiangxi and attained the Way. He later lived at Daan Monastery in Hongzhou, where the assembled multitude streamed to him. Minister Pei Xiu, governing Wanling, built a great Chan monastery and asked the master to speak the Dharma there; the master so loved Huangbo Mountain that he was named after it. He left behind the Essentials of the Mind-Seal Transmission. That work says:

'If you are a real man, look at a gongan. A monk asked Zhaozhou: Does a dog have the Buddha-nature or not? Zhaozhou said: Wu (no). Only go, throughout the six periods of the day and night, and look at this word “wu.” Investigate it by day and by night, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, whether putting on clothes or eating, whether passing waste or water — in thought after thought, gathering your spirit, guard this word “wu.” As days and months deepen, it is beaten into one piece; suddenly the heart-flower bursts into bloom, and one awakens to the crucial point of the Buddhas and patriarchs, and is no longer deceived by the tongues of all the old monks of the world; then one can open one's wide mouth: When Bodhidharma came from the West it was to raise waves where there was no wind; when the World-Honored One held up the flower, it was one great defeat. Having reached this point, what can the old lord Yama do to you — even a thousand sages are helpless against you! Do you not believe that there is such a wonder? Why so? Because even a matter feared is attended to when there is a heart! A verse says: To slip from the dust and toil is no common thing; grip tight the leading rope and make one mighty stand! But for a cold that pierces straight to the bone, how should the plum blossom give forth fragrance alone?'

[Zhaozhou] The Tang dynasty Chan master Zhaozhou Congshen. [Gathering your spirit] Rousing yourself; 'spirit' means spirit and vigor. [Grip the leading rope] A metaphor drawn from herding an ox. [Handle] Means a place to seize hold of.

[Why is this? Only because in the eighth consciousness of the student, the seeds of evil habits from countless kalpas have been perfuming within from thought to thought, flowing on continuously, with deluded thought unending, and there is nothing one can do. Therefore a single word with no flavor is given you to bite into fast; first put down at once all the deluded thoughts of inner and outer mind-and-realm. Because you cannot put them down, you are taught to hold up this huatou; it is like cutting tangled silk: one cut and it is all cut, with no further continuity — cut off consciousness and do not let it pass again. This is precisely the rule of Bodhidharma's 'extinguishing all conditions outside, no panting within, the mind like a wall.' Unless one sets to work this way, one will never see one's own Original Face. It is not teaching you to search on the sentences of the gongan and make of it a feeling of doubt, expecting to find your answer there.]

Why is this? Only because in the eighth consciousness of the student, the seeds of evil habits from countless kalpas have perfumed within from thought to thought, flowing on continuously, with deluded thought unending and nothing to be done about it. Therefore a single word with no flavor is given you to bite into fast; first put down at once all the deluded thoughts of inner and outer mind-and-realm. Because you cannot put them down, you are taught to hold up this huatou
using this one thought to meet ten thousand thoughts)

; it is like cutting tangled silk: one stroke and all is cut, with no further continuity — cut off consciousness and do not let it pass again. This is precisely the rule of the Patriarch Bodhidharma's 'extinguishing all conditions outside, no panting within, the mind like a wall.' Unless one sets to work thus, one can never see one's own Original Face. It is not teaching you to search on the sentences of the gongan, taking it as a feeling of doubt and expecting to find your answer there.

[Take Dahui, for instance: he exclusively taught looking at the huatou and applied the deadly hand, only wanting you to kill the thieving mind. As he told the assembly: "To investigate Chan one needs only to empty the mind, to paste the two characters birth-and-death on the forehead, as if one owed someone ten thousand strings of cash. In the three periods of day and three of night, in tea and in rice, when walking, standing, sitting, and lying, when exchanging courtesies with friends, in stillness and in noise, raise a huatou: Does a dog have the Buddha-nature or not? Zhaozhou said: Wu. Just keep looking here, again and again. When it has no flavor, it is like running against a wall; when it comes to the juncture, it is like a rat entering an ox's horn — then you will see the end of it. I want you to bring an enduring body-and-mind to it and wrestle with it. Suddenly the heart-flower bursts forth, illuminating the lands of the ten directions — one awakening, and it is thoroughly done." This whole passage
(these words above)

is the tongs and hammer the old man Dahui habitually used; its meaning is only that you should use the huatou to block the flowing stream of deluded thought beneath the consciousness and make it not run and — right where it does not run — look for the Original Face. It is not teaching you to search on the gongan, take it as a feeling of doubt, and seek an answer. For when he speaks of the 'heart-flower bursting forth,' how could that be gained from anywhere else?]

Take Dahui, for example, who exclusively taught looking at the huatou and applied the deadly hand (making war on greed, hatred, and delusion), wanting only that you kill the thieving mind (the mind that reaches outward). For instance, he told the assembly: 'To investigate Chan one needs only to empty the mind, to set the two characters birth-and-death on the forehead, as if one owed someone ten thousand strings of cash. In the three periods of day and three of night, in tea and in rice, walking, standing, sitting, and lying, when exchanging courtesies with friends, in stillness and in noise, raise a huatou: Does a dog have the Buddha-nature or not? Zhaozhou said: No. Just keep looking here, again and again. When it has no flavor it is like running against a wall; at the final juncture, like a rat entering an ox's horn, there is only advance and no retreat — then you will see the outcome. I want you to bring an enduring body-and-mind and wrestle with it. Suddenly the heart-flower bursts, illuminating the lands of the ten directions, and one awakening is fully complete.' This passage above is the tongs and hammer the old man Dahui habitually used; its meaning is only this: use the huatou to block the flowing stream of deluded thought beneath the consciousness so that it does not run, and right where it does not run, look for the Original Face. It is not teaching you to search on the gongan, take it as a feeling of doubt, and seek to settle it. For when he says the 'heart-flower bursts,' how could that be gained from anywhere else (from some thought)? (The Chan Barrier says: 'They roused the three hundred and sixty joints and the eighty-four thousand pores, raising a great pound of doubt through the whole body, and investigated this word “wu,” holding it day and night.')

[Thieving mind] 'Thieving mind' refers to the shadow-image of the six sense-dusts, also called consciousness-emotion, that is, the discerning mind. Chan master Zhongfeng said: 'What is the thieving mind? It is another name for consciousness-emotion, because it can rob away one's own supreme Dharma-wealth.' (Zhongfeng's Extensive Record) [Six periods] Ancient India divided a full day and night into six periods: three of day and three of night. The three of day are morning, midday, and sunset; the three of night are first night, middle night, and last night. Each such period equals four modern hours, so the six periods make twenty-four hours. [See the end] To make clear the cause-and-effect relations or some outcome of an affair. [Flowing stream of deluded thought] The arising, ceasing, and flowing of deluded thoughts. [The flowing stream of deluded thought does not run] The flowing stream of deluded thoughts comes to rest.

[As the Buddhas and patriarchs above have indicated one by one, they want you to investigate yourself, not to search for it in their mysterious and wonderful words. Today people investigating Chan and doing the work all say they are looking at a huatou and rousing a feeling of doubt. They do not know to investigate at the root; they simply seek on the huatou, seeking and seeking, until suddenly they think up a state of light, then say they have awakened, offer a verse and present it, treating it as a precious thing and thinking they have attained it — not knowing they have fallen entirely into the net of deluded views and opinions. Investigating Chan like this — does it not blind the eyes of all the people of the world to come?]

The Buddha and patriarchs above, in their one-by-one pointers, want you to investigate yourself, not to seek from their mysterious words and phrases. Today people investigating Chan and doing the work all say they look at a huatou and rouse a feeling of doubt. They do not know to investigate at the root; they only seek on the huatou (by thinking and measuring), seeking and seeking until suddenly they imagine a state of light, then say they have awakened, offer verses and present them, treating it as a precious thing, believing they have realized — not knowing they have fallen entirely into the net of deluded views and opinions. Investigating Chan like this — does it not blind the eyes of the people of the world to come?

[The young people of today, before their meditation cushion is steady, claim to have awakened to the Way, and give free rein to their mouths, playing with the spirit, reckoning it as the swiftness of the live word; they think up a few unfounded, reckless words and wild talk and call it 'a verse on the old case.' All this comes from your own deluded thinking — have you ever so much as dreamed of the ancients? If awakening to the Way were so easy for today's people, then the practice of the ancients — Changqing, who wore out seven cushions in sitting, Zhaozhou, who for thirty years did not scatter his attention — compared with these, the ancients would be the dullest-rooted of men, unfit even to carry the straw sandals of you moderns. People of overweening pride who claim to have attained what they have not attained — is this not to be feared!]

The young people of today, before their meditation cushion is steadied, claim to have awakened to the Way, and give free rein to their tongues and play with the consciousness, reckoning it as the swiftness of the live word; they think up a few unfounded, wild words and nonsense and call them 'verses on the old cases.' All this is derived from your own deluded thinking — have you ever so much as seen the ancients in a dream? If awakening to the Way came so easily to the people of today, then the conduct of the ancients — for example, the master Changqing Huileng of Fuzhou, who sat through and wore out seven cushions, and the Chan master Zhaozhou, who for thirty years never muddled his attention — compared in this way, the ancients would be the dullest-rooted people, unfit even to carry the straw sandals of you moderns. These people of overweening pride, who claim attainment without having attained — is this not fearful!

[Conduct] Practice and upholding. [To claim what one has not attained — is this not to be feared?] To claim attainment without attaining is a great false utterance. In the holy path, to speak of what one has not obtained as obtained, and to declare realization without having realized, in order to deceive the foolish and secure benefit and support — all this is called a 'great false utterance,' and its offense is very grave; after death one falls into the great hell.

[In investigating Chan and looking at the huatou, rousing the feeling of doubt is by no means dispensable. It is said: a small doubt, a small awakening; a great doubt, a great awakening; no doubt, no awakening. One need only use the feeling of doubt well; once that doubt is broken, the nostrils of the Buddhas and patriarchs are naturally strung on one cord. Take the gongan on Buddha-recitation: you should only investigate who it is who is reciting the Buddha's name; it is not doubting who the Buddha is. If you doubt who the Buddha is, then just listen to the lecturer say Amitabha Buddha, named Boundless Light, and on that suppose you have awakened, and compose a few verses on Boundless Light. If that is called awakening to the Way, then awakened minds would be as plentiful as hemp and millet. Pitiful! Pitiful!]

To investigate Chan and look at the huatou, rousing a feeling of doubt is absolutely indispensable. It is said: a small doubt brings a small awakening; a great doubt brings a great awakening; no doubt, no awakening. One need only use the feeling of doubt well; once it breaks, the nostrils of the Buddhas and patriarchs are naturally strung on one cord. For instance, in the gongan on Buddha-recitation one should only look into 'who is reciting the Buddha's name,' not doubt who the Buddha is. If one doubts who the Buddha is, then one need only listen to the lecturer say Amitabha Buddha, named Boundless Light, and on that suppose one has awakened, and compose a few verses on Boundless Light. Calling this awakening to the Way, then awakened minds would be as plentiful as hemp and grain. Pitiful! Pitiful!

[The ancients said: 'The huatou is like a tile to knock at the door — it is only to knock open the door and see the person inside the house, not to be working outside the door.' From this one sees that the doubt which rises from the huatou does not lie in the huatou, but must be at the root. Take Jiashan going to visit Chuanzi. Chuanzi asked: 'My fishing line hangs a thousand feet; the intent lies in the deep pool. When the hook is three inches from the water, how do you say it?' Jiashan was about to speak when the master knocked him into the water with a single stroke of the oar. No sooner had Jiashan climbed onto the boat than the master said again: 'Speak! Speak!' Jiashan was about to speak again when the master struck him once more. Jiashan greatly awakened and nodded three times, saying: 'The line and the silk upon the tip of the pole I leave to you to play with; not touching the clear waves, the meaning itself is other.' If Jiashan had been making his work on the hook and the line, how could Chuanzi have risked his life for him? This is the quick and convenient way by which the ancients found their way out.]

The ancients said: 'The huatou is like a tile for knocking at the door — knocking opens the door so you can see the person inside (the intrinsic nature), not that you are to be working outside the door.' From this it is clear that the doubt which rises from the huatou is not in the huatou, but must lie at the root. As when Jiashan (Shanhui) went to visit Chuanzi (Decheng). Chuanzi asked: 'My fishing line hangs a thousand feet; the intent lies in the deep pool. When the hook hangs three inches from the water, what do you say?' Jiashan was about to open his mouth when Chuanzi knocked him into the water with a single stroke of the oar. As soon as Jiashan had climbed onto the boat, Chuanzi said again: 'Speak! Speak!' Jiashan was about to speak, and Chuanzi struck him again. Jiashan greatly awakened, and nodded three times, saying: 'The line and the silk upon the pole's tip, I leave to you to play with; so long as I do not disturb the clear waves, the meaning is of itself other.' If Jiashan had been making his work on the hook and the line, how could Chuanzi have risked his own life for him? This is the quick and convenient way by which the ancients found their way out.

[Three inches from the hook] Master Hanshan's Collection of Dream Wanderings, 'Assorted Sayings from Jingshan,' says: 'Bite fast on the huatou — not that you want to clarify the huatou; you only borrow the huatou to rouse doubt and cut off deluded thinking. The investigation must be pursued apart from the huatou; only when the doubt is raised does it gain power. An ancient worthy said: "Three inches from the hook — how do you say it?" The men of old already marked it. When the doubt reaches the point that consciousness cannot reach and words cannot pass, when pressed to the extreme, a little light bursts forth, called the lightning samadhi. Just then is the time to advance; do not be delighted. If you take this as so, you rest content with little, and your whole body is covered by this bit of light, so you can no longer get out. When later it issues forth, it is all made use of by it.' [How could Chuanzi risk his life for him?] See the detail
Essentials of Chan and Pure Land
in the section on 'the heart of loyalty' regarding the note on Chuanzi.

[In former times, when the way of Chan flourished, clear-eyed teachers were everywhere. The monks of the world who investigated were many, and everywhere there was development. Moreover it was said: it is not that there is no Chan; it is only that there is no teacher. Now the Chan house has been silent for a long time. How fortunate that at once there are many who have stirred to investigate! Though there are teachers, some measure capabilities and advance tentatively, confirming according to their feelings. Students' minds are shallow, and they think they have obtained it; again they do not believe the Tathagata's holy teaching, nor seek the true path; they simply go on muddled, and take the 'winter-melon seal' as the final verdict. Not only do they wrong themselves, they also wrong others — is this not to be feared!]

In former times, when the way of Chan flourished, clear-eyed teachers were everywhere. The monks of the world who investigated were many, and everywhere there were those whose minds opened. And it was said: it is not that there is no Chan, only that there is no teacher. Now the Chan school has been silent for a long time. How fortunate that at this moment many have stirred to investigate! Although there are teachers, some measure the faculties and advance tentatively, confirming according to emotion. Students' minds are shallow and think they have obtained it; neither do they believe the Tathagata's holy teaching, nor seek the true path; they simply work in confusion and take the 'winter-melon seal' as the final verdict. Not only do they wrong themselves, they also mislead others — is this not to be feared?

[Patch-robed monk] Also called a 'patch-robed monk,' another name for a Chan monk, because Chan monks often wear a single patched robe and wander about. [Development] To realize the mind-ground, that is, awakening. [Winter-melon seal] A seal carved from the skin of a winter melon, a metaphor for false and unreal confirmation. [Seal] A stamp used as a certificate of authenticity. [Final verdict] Meaning to fix a verdict; here it means the teacher's confirmation of a student's state of realization.

[Moreover, of the magistrates and laymen of old recorded in the Transmission of the Lamp, there are only a few. Yet today's people amid the dust and toil, who observe not even the coarse precepts and are disturbed and deluded, relying on their own cleverness and having read a few 'live words' of ancient worthies, each regards himself as of the highest faculties, and whenever he meets a monk he tries his hand at the sharp word, taking himself to have awakened. Though this is the sickness of the times, it is also because our kind lead the blind and the blind follow. Now I, the old man, following the genuine essential points of the work of the Buddhas and patriarchs, discuss them with you all; the wise and accomplished will set them right on their own.]

And of the prefects and laymen of old, those recorded in the Jingde Transmission of the Lamp number only a few. Today's people amid the dust and toil, who do not keep even the coarse precepts and are muddled by deluded thinking, relying on their own small cleverness and having read a few 'live words' of the ancients, each regards himself as of the highest-rooted faculties, and when he meets a monk he contests the sharp word, thinking he has truly awakened. Though this is the sickness of the age, it is also that one blind man leads many blind. Now I, the old man, following the genuine essential points of the work of the Buddhas and patriarchs, consult with you all; the wise and accomplished will correct it on their own.

[Magistrate] A subordinate officer of the prime minister in the Zhou dynasty; later a general term for officials. [Prime minister] A Zhou dynasty title, the head of the six ministers, also called the grand steward. [The live word] A Chan-school term for a statement that is quick and sharp, leaves no trace, and is deep in meaning. The original sense of 'live word' is the trigger of a crossbow and the arrow's point; the Chan school uses it to liken a swift and profound argument and phrase. Chan teachers often use the live word, testing in dialogue the degree of another's awakening.
